summary:
Kwara stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the federal criminal law apply in the state, and in 2022 a court ruled sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the act unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide.

Kwara is not among the twelve states that adopted sharia penal law: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. No sharia penal application is documented for Ilorin or elsewhere in the state, and the sharia penal exposure recorded in those twelve states does not extend here.

The sources record no Kwara-specific arrest, prosecution, venue closure or violent incident. Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the act, which documents mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions across Nigeria, names no case in Kwara.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement of the act elsewhere in Nigeria has included mass arrests at private gatherings: Human Rights Watch records 21 young men arrested at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and never charged, part of the pattern of arbitrary arrest that followed the act's passage. No gathering-based arrest in Kwara is documented in these sources.

BBC News reported on 9 August 2024 that mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common in Nigeria, especially in the northern states, in the same reporting that covered the murder of the transgender TikToker known as 'Abuja Area Mama' in Abuja. Both the arrest pattern and that killing are documented outside Kwara; the sources place no instance of either in the state.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ+ residents of Kwara live under the federal act with no state-level protection recorded in these sources: no Kwara statute, policy or police directive offering protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is documented, and no Kwara-specific hate-crime provision appears.

Residents of Ilorin and elsewhere in Kwara face the federal criminal exposure of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sexual activity, with no sharia penal overlay. The enforcement practice documented under the same statute elsewhere in Nigeria — arbitrary arrest, extortion, detention without charge — is the practice that applies here, although no Kwara instance is recorded.

The sections of the act struck down by the 2022 ruling are unenforceable against residents nationwide, including in Kwara. The sources do not record how Kwara courts have applied that ruling, or whether residents have relied on it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 ruling on sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) has been invoked or applied in Kwara courts is unresolved in these sources; no Kwara judgment is documented.

No information is sourced on Kwara-specific police practice, conditions of detention in the state, or access to medical care and gender-affirming care for trans residents. Whether any sharia personal-status provisions of non-penal character operate in Kwara is also not sourced; only the absence of sharia penal application is documented.

The absence of recorded incidents in Kwara reflects the coverage of these sources, which are national in scope. It is not evidence that no incident has occurred, and no Kwara-level survey or monitoring data appears in the inventory.
